summary: COP31 runs late over fossil fuels, a claimed AI-assisted proof of the Riemann hypothesis, a landmark genocide ruling on Myanmar, and new talk of guarantees for Ukraine.

question.text: If a proof is checked by a computer but no human fully understands it yet, what might change about how science and maths decide something is true, and who gets trusted to say so?

read.title: Kushner says Russia OK with 'NATO-like' security pact for Ukraine: Is it?
read.summary: An explainer on what NATO's Article 5 does and does not promise, why Russia's public line differs from what the US says, and what experts think a guarantee for Ukraine could mean.

topics.heading: COP31 climate talks run past their deadline in a fight over fossil fuels
topics.summary: The UN climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, ran into Saturday after a revised draft deal dropped every mention of fossil fuels.[^1][^3] The summit's Turkish president says a new text is expected today, but oil producers and countries pushing for a phase-out remain far apart.[^1][^2]

lead.title: Fossil fuel row sees COP31 talks spill into overtime

alsoReported.title: COP31 climate talks spill into overtime as nations quarrel over fossil fuels
COP31 runs into overtime over fossil fuel dispute

article: COP31, the yearly UN climate conference, was due to end on Friday in Antalya, Türkiye. Instead, negotiators from nearly 200 countries kept talking into Saturday.[^1][^3] The main fight is over fossil fuels. An early draft called for speeding up the phase-out of coal, oil and gas; a shorter version released on Thursday by co-host Australia left them out entirely.[^2] Reuters reports that change came after objections from Saudi Arabia and other big oil and gas producers, and that the draft also dropped a $120 billion target for helping poorer countries adapt.[^3]

Countries on the other side pushed back hard. The EU said the text risked turning the meeting into a "fossil summit", and a dozen countries, including France, Panama and the Solomon Islands, signed a letter calling for "a clear transition away from fossil fuels".[^1][^2] Panama's environment minister has threatened to block any deal without a cap on oil production.[^2] Uganda's negotiator objected to language encouraging carbon removal, saying it lets rich countries keep producing oil and gas.[^3]

Background: at COP28 in 2023, countries agreed for the first time to "transition away" from fossil fuels. Every COP decision needs consensus, so a single bloc can water a text down. The United States is absent for a second year after President Trump ended its climate cooperation.[^3] The latest draft focuses on electrification, backed by Türkiye's goal of electricity meeting 35% of final energy demand by 2035.[^2]

Why it matters: burning fossil fuels is the main cause of warming, and the draft itself accepts that the world is projected to overshoot the 1.5C goal.[^3] COP31 president Murat Kurum said late Friday that talks were "close to the finish line".[^1] My read: a deal is likely this weekend, but whether it mentions fossil fuels at all is the test most observers will use to judge it.
topics.differences: Saudi Arabia and Venezuela argued in their speeches for a continued role for fossil fuels.[^3] The EU, Panama, France and small island states say a deal without fossil fuels is unacceptable.[^1][^2] Australia's Chris Bowen, who leads the talks, says electrification is itself the way to move away from fossil fuels.[^2]

topics.heading: A mathematician says he and an AI have proved the Riemann hypothesis, unsolved since 1859
topics.summary: Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, says he and its AI model Claude found a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, one of maths' most famous open problems.[^4] The proof exists only as computer-checked Lean code; early expert checks are encouraging, but human understanding is still far off.[^4][^5]

lead.title: Anthropic worker claims to have cracked unsolved math problem with the help of AI

alsoReported.title: Riemann hypothesis proof claimed by Anthropic mathematician

article: On Friday, Levent Alpöge, a mathematician on Anthropic's technical staff, posted a four-page note on his personal website saying he believes he has a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, made together with Claude, Anthropic's AI model.[^4] The hypothesis, posed by Bernhard Riemann in 1859, is about how prime numbers are spread out. It is one of seven Millennium Prize Problems, each with a $1 million reward.[^4]

The proof is not a normal paper. It is written in Lean, a programming language for checking proofs step by step by computer. AP reports about 17 million lines of code and more than 250,000 pages of AI-generated working, and Alpöge says it is too long and unfinished for a readable write-up.[^4][^5] AFP reports that MIT's Andrew Sutherland found all 175,187 Lean files compiled using only standard assumptions.[^5] A clean compile shows the proof is internally consistent; experts are now checking that it proves the right statement.[^5]

Early reactions are careful but striking. Rutgers mathematician Alex Kontorovich told AP the proof appears true, but added: "Does that mean I understand it? Not yet."[^4] Martin Bridson, president of the Clay Mathematics Institute, called it an announcement "of historic significance" but said reaching real understanding will be "long and difficult".[^4] Clay's rules require publication, then two years and general acceptance, so no prize could come before late 2028.[^5]

Why it matters: if it holds, a machine will have done most of the work on a problem the best human mathematicians could not crack for 167 years. That raises new questions about what counts as understanding in maths. It came a day after Anthropic's record stock market debut, and Anthropic had not commented as of AP's report.[^4] A note on this brief: it is prepared with Claude, the AI in this story, so weigh my framing with that in mind.

topics.heading: UN top court rules that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya
topics.summary: The International Court of Justice voted 9 to 6 that Myanmar's 2017 military campaign against the Rohingya was genocide, the first time it has held a state responsible for the crime.[^6][^7] The ruling is final, but the court cannot enforce it.[^6]

lead.title: The U.N.'s top court rules Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya

alsoReported.title: World Court Finds Myanmar Committed Rohingya Genocide

article: On Thursday the International Court of Justice (ICJ), the UN's top court for disputes between countries, ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, a mostly Muslim minority. Judges voted 9 to 6. It is the first time in the court's 80-year history that it has found a state responsible for genocide.[^6][^7] The case was brought by Gambia under the 1948 Genocide Convention, which lets any member country take another to court.[^6]

The case is about a 2017 military crackdown in Rakhine state. The court estimated about 10,000 Rohingya were killed and found the violence was systematic, including the burning of all or part of 392 villages. About 700,000 people fled to Bangladesh.[^6] Myanmar's military had said it was fighting insurgents; the judges rejected that explanation, and HRW notes the court found intent to destroy the group was "the only reasonable inference".[^6][^7]

The court ordered Myanmar to stop ongoing violations, investigate and punish those responsible, and pay reparations, with amounts set later. The ruling cannot be appealed.[^7] But the ICJ has no police of its own; enforcement falls to the UN Security Council, which HRW says has never used that power.[^7] Myanmar's military-backed government had not responded when NPR reported.[^6]

Why it matters: the reasoning will shape other genocide cases, including South Africa's case against Israel, lawyers and HRW say.[^6][^7] Return home is still hard: the Arakan Army, an armed group, now controls most of Rakhine. UN Secretary-General António Guterres called the ruling "a powerful recognition" of the victims, while the US State Department said it is studying it and raised doubts about the court.[^6]
topics.differences: Six of fifteen judges disagreed with the genocide finding.[^6] Myanmar's military has long described the 2017 operation as counter-insurgency; the court majority rejected that.[^7] The US says it is still assessing the ruling.[^6]

topics.heading: US envoy says Russia could accept NATO-style guarantees for Ukraine; Moscow says no
topics.summary: After a meeting of Ukraine's backers in Berlin, US envoy Jared Kushner said Russia is "comfortable" with security guarantees for Ukraine modelled on NATO's Article 5.[^8][^10] Russian officials publicly call any such arrangement unacceptable, and Zelenskyy says the allies do not yet agree on what it would mean.[^10]

lead.title: Ukraine's allies hold the line in Berlin as Kushner pushes for compromise

alsoReported.title: Kushner says Russia OK with 'NATO-like' security pact for Ukraine: Is it?
Zelenskyy identifies best security guarantee for Ukraine as proposals presented to partners

article: On Thursday about 40 countries in the "coalition of the willing", the group backing Ukraine's future security, met at the German Chancellery in Berlin with US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff.[^8][^10] Afterwards Kushner told reporters that Russia has become "comfortable" with a guarantee for Ukraine based on Article 5, NATO's promise that an attack on one member is an attack on all. He said it would have to serve US interests and go through Congress.[^8]

Moscow's public line is different. Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov called any "quasi membership" for Kyiv totally unacceptable, and Putin has said NATO membership and guarantees for Ukraine are unacceptable.[^10] Zelenskyy said NATO membership would be the best guarantee, but that there is no shared understanding yet of what Article 5-style guarantees would involve.[^9][^10] He says Ukraine is "not exchanging anything for anything" on territory, after US negotiators reportedly floated NATO entry in return for leaving Donbas.[^8]

European leaders took different lines. Macron said the question of Ukraine joining NATO should be reopened, while Germany's Merz called the same day's Trump-Putin-Xi meeting in Shenzhen a "photo op".[^8] The joint statement of Germany, France, the UK and Ukraine calls for "robust and legally binding" guarantees after a ceasefire, possibly including a European-led force, without mentioning Article 5.[^8] Poland's Donald Tusk said Poland will not send troops.[^8]

Why it matters: guarantees are the core question of any peace deal, because Ukraine fears Russia would attack again. Experts quoted by Al Jazeera note that Article 5 is a political decision, not automatic, and one called a full guarantee hard to believe.[^10] My read: talk of guarantees is moving, but the gap on territory is as wide as ever, and the same night Russia hit Kyiv's bridges.
topics.differences: Kushner (US) says Russia is comfortable with Article 5-style guarantees.[^8] Russia's deputy foreign minister and Putin say such guarantees are unacceptable.[^10] Ukraine wants NATO membership and refuses to trade land; Europe's joint statement asks for binding guarantees but does not mention Article 5.[^8][^9]

topics.heading: US Senate votes 51-48 against a measure to end the Iran war without Congress's approval
topics.summary: In the first Iran war vote since the midterms, the Senate rejected a war powers resolution 51 to 48, with three Republicans voting yes.[^11][^12] Democrats who take control in January say they will keep pushing, including through next month's funding fight.[^11]

lead.title: US Senate rejects resolution curbing Trump's Iran war powers

alsoReported.title: Senate rejects resolution to block Trump from striking Iran

article: On Thursday the US Senate rejected, 51 to 48, a resolution directing President Trump to end the war with Iran or get Congress's approval to continue it.[^12] The House had already passed it in September. Three Republicans, Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski and Rand Paul, voted yes; Democrat John Fetterman voted no.[^11][^12] It was the first major test of the war in the Senate since Democrats won both chambers on November 3.[^12]

Background: the US-Israeli war on Iran began on February 28.[^12] The 1973 War Powers Resolution is a law meant to let Congress stop a president's use of force. The White House ignored a similar resolution Congress passed in June, and it argues, citing a 1983 Supreme Court case, that such resolutions are unconstitutional.[^11]

The two sides framed the war very differently. Republican Senator Tim Sheehy called it "a war of necessity".[^11] Democrat Tim Kaine said the war's unpopularity was made clear in the election, and linked it to higher prices for food and fuel.[^12] AP notes that Vice President JD Vance is among Republicans who blamed the midterm losses on the war.[^11]

What could happen next: government funding runs out on December 12, and some Senate Democrats want to refuse a spending bill that includes money for the war.[^11] Democrats take control of Congress in January. My read: the vote shows Republicans still largely back the president for now, so pressure will shift to budgets rather than war powers votes.
topics.differences: Republicans like Sen. Sheehy say the war is necessary for US security; Democrats like Sen. Kaine say voters rejected it and it is driving up prices.[^11][^12] The White House says war powers resolutions are unconstitutional; supporters say the 1973 law requires withdrawal.[^11]
